notes.meaning: The "strong" are believers whose consciences felt free about things like food laws and special days. Paul counts himself among them. Their strength is not for showing off. It is for helping carry the weaknesses of those with tender consciences, not just putting up with them. So they must not live only to please themselves.

Each believer should aim to please his neighbor. That does not mean going along with sin or flattering people. It means seeking their real good and helping them grow strong in faith. Pleasing people for their own good is very different from being a people-pleaser.

Jesus is the great example. He did not live for his own comfort or honor. Paul quotes Psalm 69:9: the insults people threw at God landed on Christ. Many commentators also see here Christ carrying the guilt of our sins on the cross. If he bore so much for us, we can bear the small weaknesses of fellow believers.

The Old Testament was not written only for people long ago. It was written to teach us too. Scripture helps us endure hard things patiently, and it comforts and encourages our hearts. Through that endurance and comfort, we keep our hope alive.

Paul turns his teaching into a prayer, because only God can create this kind of unity. God is the true source of endurance and encouragement, and he gives them through Scripture. Paul asks for a harmony that follows Christ's example and agrees in truth, not in error. The goal is that Jewish and Gentile believers praise God together with one heart and one voice.
So welcome one another, both weak and strong, both Jew and Gentile. Do it the way Christ welcomed you: by grace, knowing your faults. When believers welcome each other in love, God gets the glory.

Christ came as a servant to the Jewish people. He kept God's promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the "patriarchs," or founding fathers, and so showed that God keeps his word. He also came so that Gentiles would praise God for his mercy, since they had no promise of their own. Paul quotes Psalm 18:49 about praising God among the nations. So neither group should look down on the other.

Paul quotes the song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:43. Even there, the nations are invited to rejoice together with God's people. The wall between them has come down, and Gentiles now share the joy of belonging to God.

Paul adds Psalm 117:1, which calls all nations to praise the Lord. He piles up these verses to show that this hope runs all through the Old Testament. People can only praise a God they know, so the call also means the nations would come to know him.

Isaiah 11:10 speaks of the "Root of Jesse." Jesse was King David's father. Isaiah pictures his family tree cut down, yet with a new shoot rising from the root. That shoot is the Messiah, Jesus, who rules over the nations, and the nations put their hope in him.

Paul prays to "the God of hope." God is both the one who gives hope and the one we hope in. Joy and peace come as we keep trusting him. Overflowing hope comes by the Holy Spirit's power, not by our own strength, so the Spirit gets the glory.
Paul had never met these believers, yet he trusts that they are good, well taught, and able to counsel one another. This is not flattery but honest praise. He did not write because he doubted them.

Paul wrote boldly in places, but only as a reminder. He did it because God had made him an apostle to the Gentiles. He describes his work like a priest's service. The Gentiles who come to faith are themselves the offering he brings to God, made holy by the Holy Spirit. These commentators read this priestly language as a word picture, not as making ministers into literal priests.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that the church has ordained priests who offer the sacrifice of the Mass. The Protestant commentators here reject that idea when they explain this verse.

notes.meaning: Paul does have reason to rejoice in his work. But his joy is "in Christ Jesus" and in the things of God, not in himself. The success belongs to God.

Paul will speak only of what Christ did through him to bring Gentiles to obey God. Christ worked through Paul's preaching and actions, through miracles ("signs and wonders"), and through the Spirit's power. The miracles confirmed that his message came from God. From Jerusalem around to Illyricum (roughly modern Croatia), he fully spread the gospel and planted churches.

Paul's honorable ambition was pioneer work: preaching where Christ was unknown, not building on someone else's foundation. Building where others had started was not wrong. Much frontier work was still waiting, and founding new churches was an apostle's special task. Pastors who come later are meant to build up what was started.
Paul quotes Isaiah 52:15. People who were never told about the Messiah will see, and those who never heard will understand. Paul saw his mission to the Gentiles as carrying out this promise.
That pioneer work is why Paul had not yet come to Rome. A church already existed there, while other places had never heard the gospel. He chose the greatest need over his own comfort.

Now there was no new ground left for Paul in those regions. So he planned to visit Rome on the way to Spain, enjoy their company for a while, and have them help send him on his journey. Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain. Some early writers said he did, but others see no clear evidence. God still honors a sincere plan, even when he redirects it.

First, though, Paul was heading to Jerusalem to serve the believers there. "Saints" simply means God's people. He was carrying money collected for those in need. He also hoped this gift would draw Jewish and Gentile believers closer together.

Churches in Macedonia (such as Philippi) and Achaia (such as Corinth) gave gladly and freely. Many believers in Jerusalem were poor, likely because of famine and persecution. The word for "contribution" means sharing: one part of Christ's body caring for another.

The Gentile churches gave willingly, yet they also owed it. The gospel and the Scriptures came to them through the Jewish people. Sharing everyday help in return for such great spiritual blessings was only fair. Giving is free, yet love makes it a debt.

"Sealed" means Paul would deliver the gift safely and honestly, as if under seal. He was careful that no one could suspect him over the money. After that he planned to go to Spain by way of Rome. In fact, he later reached Rome as a prisoner.

Paul is sure that when he comes, he will bring Christ's blessing in full and share spiritual gifts with them. He sounds unsure about his plans, but sure about God. Calvin gives another possible reading: Paul expected to find the gospel already flourishing among them.

Paul pleads with them, by Christ and by the love the Spirit creates among believers, to "strive together" with him in prayer. The word pictures a wrestler or athlete straining hard. Paul was praying for himself too, and he wanted them as partners in the struggle. Ministers depend on the prayers of God's people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic writers have reasoned that if Paul could ask living believers to pray for him, believers may also ask the saints in heaven to pray for them. Calvin strongly rejects using this verse that way.

notes.meaning: Paul asks them to pray for two things. First, that he would be kept safe from unbelieving Jews in Judea, who saw him as a traitor. Second, that the Jerusalem believers would accept the gift, since some were suspicious of him and of Gentile money. Then, if God wills, he could come to Rome with joy and be refreshed with them. God answered, but not as expected: Paul was arrested and reached Rome in chains.

Paul closes with a blessing from "the God of peace," the one who gives peace. The title fits a church troubled by divisions. "All of you" includes both the weak and the strong, joined together under one blessing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because of the "Amen" here, some scholars think the letter first ended at this verse and that chapter 16 was a separate letter. Others note that the ancient manuscripts do not support this.
